claims.text: Fair information access differs from standard classification because retrieval outputs are rank-based and involve rivalrous position allocations.
Completely ignoring protected group attributes, known as fairness through unawareness, fails to prevent discriminatory outcomes due to correlation with proxy variables.
Simultaneously equalizing multiple error-based parity metrics across groups is mathematically impossible when base rates are unequal and models are imperfect.
Presentation and popularity biases in interactive information access systems create positive feedback loops that amplify initial disparities over time.

evidence.description: Information access systems resolve utility estimates into single or multi-dimensional rankings where high-attention positions are subtractible resources allocated among candidate items.
Group identity correlates with non-sensitive variables like income or education, allowing models to learn discriminatory patterns indirectly despite attribute suppression.

The Chouldechova-Kleinberg theorem demonstrates that false positive rate parity, false negative rate parity, and positive predictive value parity cannot be simultaneously satisfied without equal group base rates or perfect prediction.

Items recommended at top positions accumulate more user interactions, which reinforces their perceived popularity and leads to increased future recommendations at the expense of non-recommended items.

methodologies.name: Multifaceted Fair Information Access Taxonomy
methodologies.description: A taxonomy categorizing fairness in information access across stakeholder groups (consumers, providers, subjects, side stakeholders), types of harms (distributional, representational), vantage points, system pipeline stages, and time scales.

limitations.text: The monograph relies primarily on legal and moral frameworks rooted in Western, particularly United States, concepts of anti-discrimination and societal bias.

Existing machine learning fairness constructs assume separate, simultaneous, and symmetric decisions, which fail to capture ranking, personalization, and interaction dynamics inherent to information access.
Fairness evaluations in the literature predominantly simplify demographic traits into single-dimensional binary attributes, failing to address complex intersectional identities.

future_work.text: Extend fair information access metrics and interventions to additional domain settings, application types, and multidimensional or intersectional axes of demographic attributes.
Develop methodologies to evaluate and mitigate the evolution of algorithmic bias over time in dynamic interactive feedback loops.
Investigate fairness concerns for additional stakeholder groups beyond consumers and providers, including information subjects and side stakeholders.
Study user and provider perceptions, expectations, and behavioral responses regarding fairness interventions in information access systems.
